w: Outdoor escalators climb the hillside of a barrio once ranked the world's most dangerous urban area; every wall beside them now carries murals of doves, raised fists and white cloths, painted by former residents who turned the 2002 military raid that scarred the neighbourhood into a story told entirely through spray paint and tour guides who lived it.
s: Escalators through a barrio's mural-covered rebirth
why: A once-notorious hillside slum reinvented itself as one of South America's most powerful open-air galleries of resilience.

w: Twenty murals wrap the facades of a hillside barrio in a labyrinth of stairways, painted in the 1990s by Chilean masters including Roberto Matta and Nemesio Antunez as an open-air museum with no walls or tickets. Steps zigzag past Pablo Neruda's La Sebastiana house, tin-roofed homes and bay views over the port city's coloured chaos.
s: An open-air museum built into a hillside barrio
why: One of the earliest and most influential open-air mural museums in Latin America, painted by the country's leading artists.

w: A cobbled alley off Rua Goncalo Afonso takes its name from a 1980s Batman graffito that started a decades-long free-for-all; local art students layered on psychedelic and cubist designs until every surface, sidewalks included, disappeared under paint. Pieces get painted over within weeks, so the alley is never quite the same gallery twice.
s: A bohemian alley repainted every few weeks
why: One of Brazil's longest-running open graffiti walls, credited with regenerating the whole Vila Madalena district.

w: Chilean-born artist Jorge Selaron began tiling the crumbling steps outside his house in 1990, using green, yellow and blue fragments for the Brazilian flag before visitors from over sixty countries started donating tiles of their own. The 215-step staircase, straddling Lapa and Santa Teresa, was never declared finished; Selaron was found dead on it in 2013.
s: 215 mosaic-tiled steps donated by the world
why: A single artist's decades-long, ever-growing folk-art staircase that became one of Rio's most photographed landmarks.

w: Over 200 murals cover this bohemian clifftop barrio, blending social commentary with pure colour; muralist Jade Rivera keeps a studio here, and the Montero Bernales bridge near the Bridge of Sighs carries the district's largest single mural space. A 2015 crackdown that whitewashed sixty works backfired badly, sparking the annual Muraliza el Barrio festival that still runs today.
s: A bohemian clifftop barrio turned open gallery
why: Grew from scattered 2000s graffiti into Lima's densest and most curated concentration of street murals.

n: El Cuento de los Loros mural
w: Muralist Martin Ron spent sixteen days with two collaborators covering a 412-square-metre facade at Holmberg and Pedro Ignacio Rivera with parrots, a giant Michelangelo's David and a skateboarding, hyperreal portrait. Painted in 2013 as the city's largest mural to date, it also hides a small tribute to the Argentine architect Clorindo Testa within its composition.
s: A four-storey hyperreal mural of parrots and David
why: Was the largest single mural in Buenos Aires when painted, a landmark of the city's hyperrealist muralism scene.

w: A former Zapotec village swallowed by Oaxaca centuries ago, its cobbled streets now carry murals by local and Zapotec artists layered onto candy-coloured colonial facades. Calaveras and jaguar motifs recur throughout, blending folk symbolism with contemporary social and environmental themes, so the barrio's painted walls read as vivid as its architecture already was.
s: Candy-coloured colonial streets full of murals
why: One of Mexico's most concentrated blends of colonial architecture and contemporary Zapotec-inflected muralism.

w: Lithuanian artist Ernest Zacharevic's 2012 mural 'Little Children on a Bicycle', a painted boy and girl astride a real bicycle bolted to the wall, launched George Town's transformation into Malaysia's street-art capital during that year's George Town Festival. Zacharevic has since returned repeatedly to restore his fading, heavily touched heritage-enclave pieces.
s: A painted boy and girl on a real bicycle
why: The single mural credited with putting Malaysian street art on the world map, named among the Guardian's best of 2013.

w: Fox Street, running through the redeveloped Jewel City blocks, carries some of the more than fifty murals commissioned when Maboneng's industrial shells were repurposed; painters were briefed simply to reflect Johannesburg's mixed cultures and people. What was derelict warehousing barely a decade earlier is now walked block by block as an open-air gallery.
s: Fifty-plus murals through a reborn industrial zone
why: Sub-Saharan Africa's densest cluster of commissioned murals, credited with regenerating a derelict inner-city precinct.

w: More than fifty large-scale works by Faith47, Falko One and other artists cover Salt River's warehouse walls, painted mainly during the annual International Public Art Festival that Baz-Art has run since 2017. The murals confront gentrification and rising rents even as they celebrate local legends, weaving South African memory into a still-gritty, still-industrial quarter.
s: Festival murals confronting a gentrifying quarter
why: Cape Town's largest sanctioned mural trail, produced by an annual festival that brings in international street artists every year.

w: Community organisers Kibera Walls for Peace and Kibera Creative Arts began painting the corrugated-iron walls of Nairobi's largest informal settlement in the 2010s, turning them into a running dialogue on poverty, violence and survival. Crews including BSQ, and the veteran tagger Bankslave, dubbed Kenya's graffiti godfather by CNN, have since carried the same visual language across the city.
s: Informal-settlement walls turned peace murals
why: A grassroots mural movement that reframed one of Africa's largest slums as a canvas for community dialogue rather than decay.

w: Since 2010 the NGO Yataal Art, Wolof for 'spreading art', has invited over a hundred Senegalese and international painters into one of Dakar's oldest quarters, asking each family's permission before a wall is touched, often in exchange for a shared dinner. Frescoes on public health, begging and the environment now cover hundreds of facades across the historic Medina.
s: A hundred-plus artists painting a historic quarter
why: A rare street-art project built on door-to-door consent from residents rather than top-down commissioning.

w: The Urban Forms Foundation has covered more than 170 gable ends since 2009, commissioning both leading Polish painters and international names such as Os Gemeos, Eduardo Kobra, Inti and Aryz to work on the city's blank post-industrial facades. Some pieces incorporate neon that only activates after dark, making Lodz one of the largest single-city mural collections in Europe.
s: 170-plus gable-end murals across a post-industrial city
why: Ranked second globally for urban art density behind New York by a 2014 survey, the largest permanent mural collection in Poland.

w: Houses crammed along the once flood-ravaged banks of the Code river carry rainbow-roofed murals and cartoon graffiti, part of a riverside kampung revival begun by architect Romo Mangunwijaya decades earlier and continued since by local painters. The colour transformed a settlement once written off as a slum into one of Central Java's most photographed street-art strips.
s: A rainbow-roofed kampung along a once-flooded river
why: One of Southeast Asia's most striking examples of street art used for genuine riverside slum regeneration.

w: A cobbled laneway off Flinders Street has carried wall-to-wall paste-ups and spray work since the 1990s, hosting international names including Shepard Fairey and Invader alongside Melbourne regulars Ha-Ha, Prism and Rone. Matt Adnate's 23-metre 'Aboriginal Boy', painted across a multi-storey wall in 2014, remains the laneway's single most photographed piece.
s: Melbourne's original wall-to-wall graffiti laneway
why: The laneway that established Melbourne's international reputation as a street-art city, still repainted almost daily.

w: A once-derelict office street was handed to international artists for the 2011 See No Evil festival, and within days its multi-storey gable ends carried some of the largest legal murals in Europe, including Nick Walker's stencil-and-satire pieces. The street sits a short walk from Banksy's stencilled 'Well Hung Lover' and anchors Bristol's claim to being Britain's street-art capital.
s: Multi-storey murals from Bristol's See No Evil festival
why: One of Europe's largest concentrations of sanctioned high-rise murals, seeding Bristol's ongoing Upfest tradition.

w: A hillside village below Naksan Park, once slated for demolition and home mostly to poor and elderly residents, was repainted by around seventy artists under a 2006 government revitalisation project. Sunflower staircases and rooftop koi fish drew crowds so heavy that in 2016 frustrated residents quietly painted over several of the most-visited murals themselves in protest.
s: A demolition-slated hillside saved by seventy muralists
why: One of the first government-led mural regenerations in Asia, and a cautionary tale about overtourism in a living neighbourhood.

w: Narrow lanes around Ki Ling Lane and Shek Chan Lane were repainted under an urban-revitalisation scheme, filling steep staircases and shophouse walls with colour; the best-known piece, near MTR exit B3, shows a girl watering plants beside a rainbow-striped stairway. The annual HKwalls festival, running since 2014, adds fresh works across the district almost every spring.
s: A rainbow staircase in a revitalised shophouse quarter
why: One of Hong Kong's densest mural concentrations, refreshed annually by the HKwalls street-art festival.

w: A narrow alley off one of Bangkok's oldest streets was the epicentre of the 2013 and 2016 Bukruk Urban Art Festivals, and most of the work has survived: Alex Face's wide-eyed rabbit character Mardi, Bonus TMC's bears and tigers, and Lolay's bone-white creatures still line the walls. Street vendors crowd the alley by day, so the murals are best seen in late afternoon light.
s: Bukruk-festival murals down a colonial-era alley
why: Bangkok's original street-art alley, still largely intact more than a decade after its founding festival.

w: Bucharest's best-known mural strip is repainted every year during the Street Delivery festival, when the road closes to traffic and artists work outdoors in front of the crowds filling it. Pisica Patrata, one of Romania's most recognised street artists, has used walls here to draw attention to the capital's neglected historic buildings, layering activism into the annual repaint.
s: A festival street repainted live every year
why: The anchor site of Bucharest's Street Delivery festival, Romania's longest-running open-air urban art event.

w: Warehouse facades along the Sava river carry some of Belgrade's most striking murals, including Remed's many-armed 'La Santa de Belgrade' and Blu's giant figure devouring a tree of corporate towers. Much of the quarter was demolished for the Belgrade Waterfront project after 2015, so several surviving murals now stand as memorials to a creative district that no longer fully exists.
s: River-warehouse murals surviving a vanished quarter
why: Serbia's most concentrated mural district, its story bound up with the controversial redevelopment that erased much of it.

w: A self-declared bohemian 'republic' across the river from Vilnius's Old Town, complete with its own constitution and a trumpet-blowing angel statue, wears murals and installations down almost every side street off Uzupio Street. The Uzupis Art Incubator anchors the scene, giving studio space to emerging artists whose work spills straight onto the surrounding facades.
s: Murals through a self-declared artists' republic
why: A mock breakaway republic where street art, sculpture and constitution-writing artists share the same few blocks.

w: As mayor from 2001, artist Edi Rama had grey communist-era apartment blocks along the Lana river repainted in bright geometric colour, calling it his 'supreme form of conceptual art'. Locals reported paying more taxes and littering less once their buildings turned orange, purple and lime green; the annual MurAL Fest has since added large figurative murals to the same boulevards.
s: Communist blocks repainted as conceptual art by a mayor
why: A rare case of a government using large-scale colour as literal civic policy, credited with lifting local morale and tax compliance.

w: Stavanger has hosted the Nuart festival since 2001, one of the oldest dedicated street-art events anywhere, drawing names like Dolk and Martin Whatson to leave permanent, legal works across the old town. Nearby Ovre Holmegate's rainbow-painted shopfronts complement the festival pieces, and Nuart's golden years from 2006 to 2016 left the city one of Europe's densest legal mural trails.
s: A rainbow street feeding Norway's oldest art festival
why: Home to one of the world's longest-running street-art festivals, which built Norway's reputation as a serious urban-art destination.

n: MIAU Unfinished Museum of Urban Art
w: A shrinking mountain village near a landfill that locals resented turned protest into invitation: since roughly 2013 the MIAU festival has housed and fed visiting artists in exchange for murals on its old stone houses, filling the streets with painted robots, giant cats and cyborgs. Deliberately called 'unfinished', the free open-air museum keeps adding new walls every summer.
s: A mountain village that painted away its stigma
why: A depopulating rural village that reversed its decline through an annual, resident-hosted mural festival with no gallery walls at all.

w: In June 2014 the Paris gallery Itinerrance brought 150 artists from 30 countries to the whitewashed village of Erriadh, using over 4,500 spray cans to paint 250 murals across its traditional Djerban architecture in just ten days. Giant letters spelling 'THE HOOD' mark the entrance; more than 300 works now cover the village, drawing visitors to what was once a quiet island backwater.
s: 150 artists painted an entire whitewashed village
why: One of the largest single street-art interventions ever staged, transforming a traditional village into an open museum in ten days.

w: Graffiti has covered this bohemian square's walls since the late 1980s, tolerated here more openly than almost anywhere else in the city, where locals say artists paint 'pretty much anywhere'. A landmark corner building on Rue Pastoret carries one of Thoma Vuille's grinning Monsieur Chat characters, a recurring tag the Swiss-French artist has left across Marseille since 1997.
s: A bohemian square where graffiti goes almost anywhere
why: Marseille's longest-tolerated open graffiti zone, painted continuously since the late 1980s.

w: Known during the 2011 uprising as the Street of the Eyes of Freedom, the walls beside Tahrir Square filled with portraits of protesters killed by security forces, including Bakr's 'Mothers of the Martyrs'. Authorities whitewashed the murals repeatedly through 2011 and 2012, and artists kept returning to repaint them, turning one stretch of wall into a running argument over memory.
s: Revolution murals repeatedly painted and erased
why: The clearest physical record of Egypt's 2011 revolution, fought over in paint between artists and the state for years afterward.
